name: Cat's claw (Uncaria tomentosa)
short: Case report, review: acute interstitial nephritis (kidney inflammation) after cat's claw, once with diet shakes containing it. Review: raised HIV-drug levels. Small cancer trials: tolerated by most.
text: A review of herb-induced kidney toxicity states that acute allergic interstitial nephritis was diagnosed after intake of Peruvian cat's claw, and a 2022 case report describes biopsy-proven acute interstitial nephritis, with serum creatinine rising from 0.7 to 3.6 mg/dL, in a person on a strict ketogenic diet using over-the-counter diet shakes that contained cat's claw (the abstract does not list the shakes' other contents); kidney function improved to near baseline after the shakes were stopped and corticosteroids were given. A systematic review of human studies and case reports of supplement interactions with antiretroviral medicines found that cat's claw significantly increased antiretroviral levels and said patients should be monitored for adverse effects when the two are combined; the abstract does not name the antiretrovirals. In small cancer studies, a randomized trial in 43 people with colorectal cancer receiving chemotherapy reported no toxic effects when cat's claw was added for six chemotherapy cycles, and a phase II study (no control group is described) in 51 people with advanced solid tumours found the dry extract was well tolerated by most patients. A toxicology review found that animal studies did not indicate severe toxicity from oral cat's claw preparations, and noted more generally that experimental results often depended on the preparation used.
